questions.q: How does the brain store information, according to Kurzweil?
a: In ordered sequences that one cue can trigger
In isolated files sorted by importance
In random clusters that fade over time
In a single unified memory bank
questions.why: Lesson one says memories are catalogued step by step, so a small hint can bring back the whole pattern.

questions.q: Why is reciting the alphabet backwards harder than forwards?
a: Memories are stored in order, so starting midway is harder
The letters sound different in reverse order
People practice the forward version more often
Reverse speech uses a different brain area
questions.why: Lesson one uses the alphabet and piano pieces to show that sequences are easier to recall from the beginning.

questions.q: What does a pattern recognizer consist of?
a: About one hundred neurons working together
About one thousand connected synapses
A single cortical column
Millions of scattered neurons
questions.why: Lesson two says each recognizer has roughly 100 neurons, and the neocortex contains around 300 million of them.

questions.q: Where does the brain create emotions such as anger and desire?
a: In the neocortex, through spindle cells
In the amygdala, through fear circuits
In the hippocampus, through memory cells
In the cerebellum, through motor pathways
questions.why: Lesson two says spindle cells in the neocortex produce strong feelings and connect distant brain regions.

questions.q: What makes Siri seem more human than simple voice recognition?
a: It uses keywords and context rather than exact phrases
It stores every sentence a user has said
It imitates the user's accent and tone
It asks a person to type each request
questions.why: Lesson three says Siri looks for keywords and context, so it can understand a request however it is phrased.
